lessons.title: Splitting Equity Among Co-Founders: Frameworks That Prevent Fights

children.text: Co-founder equity is decided in an hour, usually over coffee, usually before anyone knows what the work will look like. It is then argued about for years. The split itself is rarely the problem. The problem is that it was set for the past, for who had the idea and who made the first pitch deck, when it should have been set for the future, for who is going to carry this company for the next five years.

body.text: Equity pays for the work still to come, not for the work already done. Split it on a defensible basis, write it down, and put vesting behind it. A split without vesting is not a decision, it is a hope.

children.text: The Equal Split Is Usually a Conversation Being Avoided

A clean 50:50 or 33:33:33 feels fair and takes ten seconds. Sometimes it genuinely is right, when two people are leaving comparable jobs, putting in comparable money and doing comparable work. Often it is chosen because the alternative is an awkward conversation about who is contributing more. That conversation does not disappear. It resurfaces in year two, when one person is working weekends and the other is not.

columns.label: Equal split
points: Fast, feels fair and avoids an early confrontation
Works well when contributions really are comparable
Can deadlock decisions when two founders hold 50% each
Breeds resentment if effort diverges later
Investors ask why the split does not match the roles they see

columns.label: Weighted split
points: Forces an honest conversation while the stakes are still small
Reflects commitment, role and money actually put in
Gives a clear answer to "why do you own more than me?"
Takes longer and can feel confrontational at first
Needs documenting properly, or it is worthless

body.text: Two co-founders at 50:50 with no tie-breaker is a governance problem, not just an emotional one. Ordinary resolutions need a majority of votes cast, and a deadlocked board or shareholder vote can stall hiring, fundraising and even bank mandates. If you choose equal ownership, agree a deadlock mechanism in the founders' agreement before you need one.

children.text: Most founder disputes come from over-weighting one factor: the idea. An idea has almost no value on its own, and the person who had it rarely built it alone. Here is a more honest weighting, with the reasoning behind each factor.

body.caption: A defensible weighting of founder contributions

cells: Full-time commitment
The scarcest input. A full-time founder is betting their career; a part-time one is not
Role criticality going forward
Who the company cannot function without over the next three years
Capital contributed
Real money at real risk, though often better handled as debt or a priced instrument
Domain expertise and network
Shortens the path: customers, hiring, regulatory know-how
The original idea
Worth something, but only a fraction of what execution is worth

children.text: A Worked Split: Three Co-Founders in Bengaluru

MetroMandi is a fictional B2B produce marketplace. Anjali left a ₹40 lakh product role to be CEO. Vikram left a ₹30 lakh engineering job to be CTO. Sameer keeps his consulting practice, contributes about a day a week and has put ₹20 lakh of his own money in. Each founder is scored out of 10 on each factor, and the weighted totals decide the split.

cells: Full-time commitment
Role criticality
Capital contributed
Domain expertise and network
Original idea
Weighted total
Share of total (1,935)

content.caption: A weighted scorecard in one line

children.text: Percentages: 750 ÷ 1,935 = 38.76%, 725 ÷ 1,935 = 37.47%, 460 ÷ 1,935 = 23.77%. The founders round these to 39%, 37% and 24%, which on 10,000 shares at incorporation means 3,900, 3,700 and 2,400 shares. Round to whole share counts, never to awkward fractions.

The scorecard is not magic. Its value is that it converts a feelings argument into a numbers argument. If Vikram thinks he should have more, he has to argue that a specific score is wrong, which is a conversation you can actually have.

body.text: Look hard at Sameer. He gets 24% of the company largely because he wrote a ₹20 lakh cheque, but he works one day a week. Three rounds later that is still a large stake held by someone not building the business, which is exactly the dead equity that makes Series A investors nervous. Money is usually better brought in as a loan or a priced instrument than paid for in founder equity.

body.title: Sameer's ₹20 lakh: two ways to take it

columns.label: As founder equity
points: Simple at incorporation, no paperwork beyond the share allotment
Permanently converts cash into a large ownership stake
The stake keeps growing in value while the contribution stays flat
Creates dead equity if he never goes full-time

columns.label: As a loan or convertible instrument
points: Cash is repaid, or converts at the next round's price
His equity then reflects his work, not his bank balance
Keeps the founder cap table clean for future investors
Needs documentation and a company secretary's help to get right

body.title: Recompute Vikram's share
body.prompt: Using the MetroMandi scorecard, Vikram's weighted total is 725 and the three founders' totals add to 1,935. What is Vikram's share of the company before rounding? Answer to two decimal places.
body.explanation: 725 ÷ 1,935 × 100 = 37.47%. Notice how close this is to Anjali's 38.76% even though she scored higher on the idea and on role criticality. Full-time commitment dominates the scorecard, which is usually the right outcome.

children.text: Indian Specifics That Catch Founders Out

body.caption: Five India-specific traps in founder splits

cells: Shares held in a relative's name for convenience
Ownership does not match reality and can create serious legal exposure
Hold shares in the actual owner's name from day one
A co-founder still serving notice at an old employer
Employment contracts may claim work done during that period, including code and IP
Wait for the release letter, or get written clearance, before assigning IP to the company
An NRI or foreign co-founder
Share issues to non-residents must follow FEMA pricing and reporting rules
Plan the structure with a CA before allotment, not after
A co-founder joining after a priced round
Shares issued cheaply once a fair market value exists can create a tax charge for the recipient
Use ESOPs or a properly valued issue, and take a CA's view first
Split agreed only over WhatsApp
Nothing is enforceable and memories differ
Sign a founders' agreement and reflect it in the shareholders' agreement and articles

body.label: The split is only half the decision
body.context: A 39% stake that vests over four years with a one-year cliff is a fair deal for everyone. The same 39% with no vesting hands a departing founder a permanent claim on a company they stopped building. Lesson 2.2 covers how to set this up.

stats.label: Founders' combined stake
stats.context: Before any ESOP pool or outside round

body.title: Which argument holds up?
body.question: Four co-founders are arguing for a larger share. Which claim is the strongest basis for more equity?
options: "It was my idea, I thought of it two years ago"
"I am the only one leaving a full-time job and I will run this daily for the next five years"
"I introduced us to a potential customer last month"
"I am the oldest and most experienced person here"
body.explanation: Equity buys future commitment. The founder giving up salary and career optionality to run the company full-time is taking the largest ongoing risk. An idea, one introduction or seniority are all worth something, but none of them survive contact with five years of execution.

body.title: Name the problem
body.textWithBlank: A large stake held by a co-founder who has stopped contributing to the company is called ___ equity.
body.explanation: Dead equity demotivates the people still building the company and is one of the first things a Series A investor looks for on a cap table.

body.title: The co-founder who arrived eight months late
body.scenario: You and one co-founder incorporated a Pune fintech eight months ago at 55:45 and have been full-time throughout, with 10,000 shares issued. A former colleague now wants to join as a third co-founder and head of growth. She is excellent, will be full-time, and is asking for an equal one-third share because "co-founders should be equal." The company has revenue, a working product and a term sheet conversation starting next month.
body.prompt: How do you respond, and what structure would you propose?
body.modelAnswer:
The principle: she is joining a company that already has a product, revenue and risk removed. An equal share would pay her for eight months of work she did not do, and would dilute both existing founders by roughly a third each.

What to propose:
1. A meaningful but smaller stake, typically in the high single digits to low teens for a strong post-incorporation hire at this stage, sized against what she will own after the next round rather than today.
2. Full vesting over four years with a one-year cliff, on the same terms the two of you should already be on.
3. Performance-linked top-ups: an additional tranche if specific growth milestones are met over the next 18 months. This closes the gap between her ask and your offer without giving it away upfront.
4. Consider ESOPs rather than founder shares if she wants a lower-risk entry, though a true co-founder role usually warrants equity.

The traps to check first:
1. Because the company now has revenue and a term sheet, a fair market value arguably exists. Shares issued to her far below that value can create a tax charge in her hands. Take a CA's view on the issue price and structure before allotment.
2. Confirm your authorised capital covers the new shares, or start the SH-7 process now.
3. Document everything in an amended founders' agreement and shareholders' agreement before the term sheet conversation, because an unresolved third co-founder is a diligence problem.

The conversation to have: explain that the split reflects when each person took risk, not seniority, and that vesting protects her as much as it protects you.

body.title: Running the split conversation properly
steps: Agree the factors and their weights before anyone sees a single score.
Score each founder independently, then compare and argue about specific numbers, not feelings.
Decide whether cash contributions should be equity at all, or a loan or convertible instrument instead.
Round to clean percentages and whole share counts.
Attach vesting with a cliff to every founder, including yourself.
Agree a deadlock mechanism if any two people can block each other.
Put it in a signed founders' agreement, then reflect it in the shareholders' agreement and articles of association.
Agree in advance how the split gets revisited if someone's role or commitment changes.

cards.definition: The contract between co-founders covering equity split, roles, vesting, IP assignment and what happens if someone leaves.
A method of splitting equity by scoring each founder on weighted contribution factors and dividing by the total.
A significant stake held by someone no longer contributing to the company.
An agreed tie-breaker, such as a casting vote or mediation clause, for when equal owners cannot agree.
The written transfer of intellectual property created by founders to the company, without which the company may not own its own product.
Shares issued under the Companies Act, 2013 to directors or employees for know-how or value addition, subject to their own conditions and limits.

points: Equity pays for future commitment, not for whose idea it was.
An equal split is fine when contributions are genuinely equal, but it is often a way to avoid a hard conversation.
Weight full-time commitment and forward-looking role criticality most heavily. The idea deserves the least.
A weighted scorecard turns an argument about fairness into an argument about specific scores, which is far easier to resolve.
Cash brought in by a founder is usually better structured as a loan or convertible instrument than as founder equity.

Watch for India-specific traps: shares in relatives' names, notice periods and IP, FEMA rules for non-resident founders, tax on cheap shares issued after a valuation exists, and splits agreed only on WhatsApp.
No split is safe without vesting, a cliff and a signed founders' agreement.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal, tax or investment advice. MetroMandi and the founders described are fictional, and all scores, weights and percentages are illustrative rather than a standard. Tax treatment of shares issued below fair market value, sweat equity rules, and FEMA requirements for non-resident shareholders change over time and depend on your facts. Consult a qualified chartered accountant, company secretary or lawyer before agreeing or issuing founder equity.
